title: Methodology
text:
Primary: Was greater pre-pandemic dependence on international tourism associated with more severe 2020 GDP contractions among Caribbean, Pacific, and AIMS small island developing states?
Secondary: Did the most tourism-dependent economies recover to their 2019 real GDP levels by 2022–2023?



This is a cross-sectional exploratory analysis. The unit of analysis is the economy (one row per country). The approach is descriptive and associational: we examine whether a pre-pandemic characteristic (tourism dependence) predicts an outcome (2020 GDP growth) using bivariate OLS regression and rank correlation.
This analysis does not establish causation. No controls for confounders (fiscal buffers, governance quality, pre-existing recession, pandemic response policy, population size, or economic structure) are included. The analysis is deliberately kept bivariate to maintain transparency about what the data show before additional assumptions are introduced.

text:
Candidate Universe and SIDS Classification

Source authority
The candidate universe was constructed from the UN Office of the High Representative for the Least Developed Countries, Landlocked Developing Countries and Small Island Developing States (UN-OHRLLS) list of SIDS, retrieved November 2026 (source).


Classification categories

Definition

Sovereign states formally listed as SIDS by UN-OHRLLS. Includes Cook Islands and Niue, which are sovereign states in free association with New Zealand and are not UN General Assembly members but appear on the SIDS list.

Associate members of UN Regional Commissions included in the SIDS group; mostly non-sovereign territories

Classification discrepancies documented

Cook Islands and Niue: Not UN General Assembly members. Included under “OHRLLS-listed SIDS” with an explicit note. Do not have WDI coverage.
Bahrain: Not on the current OHRLLS list. Previously appeared on some SIDS lists. Excluded.
BES: Dutch special municipalities. Included as “Other island economy.” No WDI coverage.

title: Methodology
text:
Sample Definitions

Fixed-sample principle
Sample membership is determined by 2017–2019 indicator availability plus 2020 GDP growth availability. This definition is fixed and does not change when baseline windows are extended or narrowed. The 2017–2019 window was used for sample definition because it is the most recent pre-pandemic three-year period available for both indicators.


Four principal samples








Sample
Criterion
N




Candidate universe
All 58 economies
58


Tourism-data sample
Any tourism indicator, 2017–2019
48


OWID shock sample
OWID vspend (2017–19) + 2020 GDP growth
29


WDI shock sample
WDI receipts (2017–19) + 2020 GDP growth
35


Common sample
Both indicators (2017–19) + 2020 GDP growth
24


Recovery sample
OWID shock sample + real GDP (2019 + ≥1 later year)
29





Excluded economies (and why)
Economies not in any shock sample are excluded because they lack either: - A usable pre-pandemic tourism baseline (AIA, GLP, MTQ, BES, COK, NIU: no WDI coverage; BLZ, TCA: no OWID vspend data for 2017–2019). - 2020 GDP growth data.
Exclusion is based on data availability, not substantive selection. These economies are documented in data/processed/country_coverage.csv.

title: Methodology
text:
Baseline Windows

Two specifications








Window
Years
Rationale




Primary (2015–2019)
Up to 5 years
A broader baseline is less sensitive to an atypical single year; more stable estimate of structural dependence


Sensitivity (2017–2019)
Up to 3 years
Most recent pre-pandemic conditions; used for sample definition





Transparency about window selection
The 2015–2019 primary window was evaluated after observing the 2017–2019 results. This is not preregistered research. The primary specification was not selected before examining the data. This is documented explicitly, and both specifications are reported in full (see Analysis, Table A5). The two specifications produce nearly identical results for the OWID indicator.


Baseline construction
For each economy and each indicator, the baseline is the arithmetic mean of available annual observations within the window. A country with 4 out of 5 possible years contributes a 4-year mean. Medians are computed as supplementary descriptive statistics (included in output tables) but are not used as primary regression inputs.
No imputation. Missing annual observations are not filled. Economies with zero observations in a window do not contribute a baseline; this could reduce N below the fixed-sample definition only if an economy had observations in 2017–2019 but none in 2015–2016 (which does not occur in these data).


Thin baselines
Economies with only one annual observation in the baseline window are flagged as “thin baseline” in all figures (open circles) and tables. Kiribati is the thin-baseline economy in both the OWID vspend samples (1 observation in 2015–2019 and 1 in 2017–2019). Sensitivity analyses excluding Kiribati (see sensitivity table) show minimal effect on results.

title: Methodology
text:
Shock Model Specification

Outcome variable
2020 annual GDP growth (%) from WDI NY.GDP.MKTP.KD.ZG. This is the percentage change in constant-price GDP from 2019 to 2020. It captures the aggregate economic shock of the pandemic year.
Limitations of this choice: - Annual GDP growth aggregates a full calendar year. COVID-19 travel restrictions began at different times in different economies, and some may have had partial within-year recovery. - GDP growth is not the only dimension of economic harm; unemployment, poverty, and debt are not captured. - Some economies had pre-existing recessions that 2020 GDP growth conflates with the COVID shock.


Explanatory variable
Pre-pandemic tourism-dependence baseline (% of GDP or % of exports), computed as described above.


Estimation
Bivariate OLS: gdp_growth_2020 ~ baseline_tourism_dependence
This is the simplest possible linear specification. No interaction terms, no controls, no fixed effects. This is intentional: the goal is to describe the raw association transparently before introducing model complexity.


Eight principal models



Dimension
Levels




Indicator
OWID visitor spending (% GDP); WDI receipts (% exports)


Sample
OWID shock sample; WDI shock sample; Common sample


Window
2015–2019; 2017–2019



Models 1–4 use the 2015–2019 baseline; Models 5–8 use 2017–2019. All eight are reported. No model is suppressed. Model preference should not be inferred from which produces the most significant p-value.


Multiple comparison adjustment
Holm’s step-down procedure is applied across all 8 principal p-values. This is reported for transparency, not as a definitive decision criterion. The 8 models are not independent (overlapping samples and related outcomes), so the Holm adjustment is conservative.


Influential observations
Cook’s distance is computed for all models. The conventional threshold 4/N is used to flag influential observations. Maldives (MDV) is consistently the most influential in OWID models (Cook’s D ≈ 0.36–0.39). Timor-Leste (TLS) is influential in WDI receipts models.
Excluding influential observations is reported as a labeled diagnostic sensitivity analysis. Influential observations are not removed from primary models. The Maldives is an economically meaningful data point — an economy with genuine extreme tourism dependence that experienced one of the largest 2020 contractions.

title: Methodology
text:
Coverage-Restricted Sensitivity
A secondary sensitivity analysis restricts each sample to economies with at least 3 annual observations in the relevant baseline window. This tests whether thin-baseline economies drive the results.
The most consequential case is S5 (WDI receipts, 2017–2019, WDI sample, N=35 → 21): 14 economies are excluded because WDI 2019 receipts data is missing (the baseline can only be computed from 2017 and 2018). The restricted N=21 sample still shows a negative slope (−0.143) but with weaker evidence (p = 0.055). This primarily reflects the severe reduction in sample size rather than an absence of pattern.

title: Methodology
text:
Recovery Index

Construction
Recovery_index_t = (Real_GDP_t / Real_GDP_2019) × 100
Computed separately for aggregate real GDP (NY.GDP.MKTP.KD) and per-capita real GDP (NY.GDP.PCAP.KD). A value of 100 means the economy has exactly returned to its 2019 level; above 100 means it has exceeded it.


Pre-pandemic baseline: 2019
The reference year is 2019, the last full year before COVID-19 travel restrictions. This is the most natural pre-pandemic comparison point. 2015–2018 observations are included to show the pre-pandemic trend.


Comparison year: 2023
The primary recovery comparison year is 2023, the most recent year with near-complete data for the sample (28/29 economies). 2024 data exists for 28 economies but is preliminary for some; 2025 data exists for 22 economies only.
Annual sample sizes vary across the recovery period and are shown explicitly in Figure 7. Cross-economy recovery comparisons at 2025 are not made because the 2025 sample (N=22) is not representative of the full shock sample.


Aggregate vs. per-capita distinction
These are not interchangeable. 19/28 economies recovered aggregate real GDP by 2023; 17/28 recovered real GDP per capita. The 2-economy gap reflects population growth in some Pacific economies. The Field Note reports both; claims about recovery should specify which measure is being used.

Rendering the site
quarto render
This renders all four pages to docs/. The site is published from docs/ on the main branch via GitHub Pages.


World Bank API
WDI data is retrieved using wbstats::wb_data(). Future runs may retrieve updated data (particularly as WDI receipts lag resolves and 2025 real GDP estimates become final). The current retrieval date is recorded in data/raw/worldbank/wdi_retrieval_metadata.txt.


OWID data
OWID CSV files in data/raw/ are fixed downloads from January–July 2026. They will not automatically update. To retrieve updated data, download fresh CSVs from the OWID grapher and replace the files in data/raw/.

title: Technical Analysis
text:
Indicator Comparison








Figure 2: OWID visitor spending (% GDP) vs. WDI tourism receipts (% exports), 2015–2019 averages. The two indicators are correlated but not interchangeable — they divide by different denominators and measure related but distinct economic concepts.





The Pearson correlation between the two indicators (across economies with both) is approximately 0.77, and the Spearman rank correlation is 0.86. They produce similar rankings but material differences for some economies. The WDI receipts/exports denominator amplifies the apparent dependence of export-intensive small economies, while the OWID visitor spending/GDP denominator captures the share of overall economic activity attributable to visitors.

Recovery vs. tourism dependence








Figure 6: Pre-pandemic visitor spending vs. 2023 real GDP index (2019=100). No statistically significant association (Pearson r = 0.18, p = 0.36, N = 28). Tourism-dependent economies had both the worst shocks and the strongest recoveries.





The absence of a significant association between tourism dependence and the 2023 recovery index (Figure 6) is not evidence that tourism dependence is harmless or that the shock was ultimately irrelevant. It reflects the fact that the same sectors that collapsed in 2020 — international tourism and hospitality — were also the sectors that recovered as travel rebounded. Economies with high visitor spending contracted sharply in 2020 and rebounded sharply from 2021 onward, producing a near-symmetrical pattern in aggregate GDP terms.
Per-capita recovery tells a more nuanced story: 17 of 28 economies had recovered GDP per person by 2023, compared with 19 of 28 for aggregate GDP. The 2-economy gap reflects continued population growth in some Pacific economies, where total output recovered but output per person had not yet returned to 2019 levels.

See Data Dictionary for source documentation and Methodology for research design.

title: Island Time, Interrupted
text:
For small island economies built on sun, sand, and sea, COVID-19 was not merely a public health emergency — it was an economic earthquake. International borders closed. Flights stopped. Hotels emptied. In places where tourism accounts for 20, 30, or 60 percent of economic activity, the shutdown of international travel meant something close to the shutdown of the economy itself.
This field note examines one specific question: Did economies that were more dependent on international tourism before the pandemic experience steeper economic contractions in 2020?
The answer, for the indicator that best measures exposure, is yes — and the association is strong enough to survive multiple robustness checks. But the story does not end with the shock. By 2023, most affected economies had returned to their 2019 GDP levels, and many of the hardest-hit had also made the fastest recoveries.
The geographic scope covers 58 candidate economies drawn from all three UN Small Island Developing States regions: the Caribbean, the Pacific, and the AIMS group (Atlantic, Indian Ocean, Mediterranean, and South China Sea). The primary analytical sample comprises 29 economies with matched pre-pandemic tourism data and 2020 economic output.

title: Island Time, Interrupted
section: Tourism Dependence: Who Was Most Exposed?
text:
Tourism Dependence: Who Was Most Exposed?
International visitor spending — the money foreign tourists spend in a destination country, measured relative to the size of that economy — varies enormously across the SIDS universe.
At the top of the dependence ladder sit economies where the entire economic structure revolves around visitors: the Maldives, Aruba, Sint Maarten, Seychelles, and Antigua and Barbuda all had pre-pandemic visitor spending exceeding 40 percent of GDP.
At the other end are economies where other sectors dominate: Guinea-Bissau, Suriname, Kiribati, Papua New Guinea, Trinidad and Tobago, and Cuba.








Figure 1: International visitor spending as a share of GDP, 2015–2019 average. Source: OWID / UN Tourism. Each bar represents one economy in the primary shock sample (N = 29). Open circles indicate thin baseline (Kiribati, 1 year of data).

title: Island Time, Interrupted
section: The 2020 Shock: Did Dependence Predict Vulnerability?
text:
The 2020 Shock: Did Dependence Predict Vulnerability?








Figure 2: Pre-pandemic visitor spending (2015–2019 avg.) vs. 2020 GDP growth. OLS regression line with 95% confidence band. Maldives (MDV) is the most influential observation. Open circle = Kiribati (thin baseline). Source: OWID / UN Tourism; WDI NY.GDP.MKTP.KD.ZG.





The association is clear and statistically robust. Across the primary shock sample (N=29), each additional percentage point of visitor spending relative to GDP was associated with approximately 0.31 percentage points of additional GDP contraction in 2020.
The relationship explains about 41% of the variance in 2020 GDP growth across these economies (R² = 0.414).

Robustness
This finding holds across:

Baseline window. Substituting the 2015–2019 mean with the narrower 2017–2019 mean produces nearly identical results (slope = -0.32, R² = 0.428).
Sample restriction. Analyzing only the 24 economies with data in both the OWID visitor spending and WDI tourism receipts series (the “common sample”) strengthens rather than weakens the association (R² = 0.489).
Exclusion of Kiribati. The one thin-baseline economy (Kiribati, with only 1 year of pre-pandemic data) barely affects the results when removed.



The Maldives
The Maldives is the most influential single observation. With visitor spending approximately 59% of GDP (2015–2019 average) before the pandemic and a GDP contraction of approximately 33% in 2020, the Maldives sits far to the right and far below the horizontal zero line. Excluding it reduces R² from approximately 0.41 to 0.31, but the direction and statistical significance of the association remain intact. The story does not hinge on the Maldives — it is consistent with the broader pattern.


A note on the complementary indicator
A second measure of tourism dependence — WDI international tourism receipts as a share of total exports (ST.INT.RCPT.XP.ZS) — produces weaker results in the full indicator-specific sample (R² = 0.10, p = 0.06) but a moderate association on the common sample (R² = 0.23, p = 0.02). The two indicators measure related but conceptually distinct things: one divides tourism receipts by total GDP, the other by total exports of goods and services. The WDI receipts series contains no observations beyond 2020 in the current retrieval, likely reflecting a change in UN Tourism data dissemination rather than a simple publication lag, which limits its use for post-pandemic tracking. See the Analysis and Data Dictionary pages for full indicator comparisons.






ImportantCorrelation, not causation



This analysis documents a cross-sectional association. It cannot establish that tourism dependence caused the observed GDP contractions. Many factors — fiscal buffers, economic structure, pandemic response, pre-existing recession, population size — are not accounted for. The association may partly reflect confounders. Interpret it as evidence of economic exposure, not a simple mechanistic claim.

title: Island Time, Interrupted
section: Recovery: Rebound, Recovery, and What’s Missing
text:
Recovery: Rebound, Recovery, and What’s Missing








Figure 3: Real GDP trajectories, 2015–2025. Index: 2019 = 100. Each line is one economy, coloured by region. The horizontal line marks the 2019 baseline. Numbers at bottom show how many economies have data each year. Source: WDI NY.GDP.MKTP.KD (constant 2015 USD). 2025 data are preliminary estimates for a subset of economies.





By 2023, 19 of 28 economies with available data had returned to or exceeded their 2019 aggregate real GDP level. Most of the Caribbean and AIMS economies recovered relatively quickly; Pacific economies were more mixed.
However, aggregate GDP recovery and per-capita recovery are not the same thing. When measured by real GDP per capita, the count of recovered economies by 2023 is 17 of 28 — two fewer than the aggregate count. The gap runs in both directions:

Four economies (Comoros, Papua New Guinea, Seychelles, and Vanuatu) had restored their aggregate GDP to 2019 levels by 2023 but had not restored GDP per capita — because population growth in those economies outpaced economic growth.
Two economies (Marshall Islands and Puerto Rico) show the opposite: their GDP per capita had recovered, but aggregate GDP had not — consistent with net population decline in both cases. Puerto Rico’s aggregate index in 2023 was approximately 99.8, just below the threshold; its per-capita index was approximately 103.

These distinctions matter. Aggregate and per-capita recovery are not interchangeable, and the direction of the gap varies by economy.

The non-recovery economies
Nine economies had not recovered to 2019 aggregate real GDP by 2023: Cuba (index ≈ 90), Curaçao (95), Suriname (86), Trinidad and Tobago (93), Tuvalu (89), Marshall Islands (93), Solomon Islands (97), Antigua and Barbuda (99), and Puerto Rico (99.8 — ). For several of these, the challenge preceded or extended well beyond COVID-19.


Tourism dependence and recovery: no simple second act
Does pre-pandemic tourism dependence predict how quickly an economy recovered? The evidence is clear: no significant association exists between the pre-pandemic visitor spending share and the 2023 recovery index (Pearson r = 0.18, p = 0.36).
The reason this association is absent is important. The most tourism-dependent economies — the Maldives, Seychelles, Bahamas, Aruba — experienced the steepest 2020 contractions, but they also benefited most from the return of international travel from 2021 onward. The shock and the rebound are mechanistically linked: the same exposure that created the vulnerability also drove the recovery once borders reopened.
This is not the same as saying tourism dependence produces resilience. It means that 2023 aggregate GDP recovery is an incomplete measure of economic well-being. It does not capture employment, inequality, debt accumulation, population change, or the quality of recovery. See the Analysis page for the full recovery coverage table and trajectory details.

title: Island Time, Interrupted
text:
What This Tells Us
Before COVID-19, the tourism-dependent small island economies were not simply at risk in theory — they were structurally exposed. When the pandemic shut down international travel, the economies most reliant on visitor spending contracted the most, and the scale of the association was large enough to be visible across a diverse set of 29 economies spanning three ocean regions.
By 2023, most had recovered their pre-pandemic GDP levels, though aggregate recovery masked meaningful divergence in per-capita terms and left a non-trivial set of economies still below their 2019 baseline.
The central empirical finding is that international visitor spending as a share of GDP is a strong predictor of the severity of the 2020 economic shock across SIDS. The WDI tourism receipts/exports measure captures a related but distinct concept and produces a weaker, less consistent result. Using the wrong indicator matters.
There is much this analysis cannot tell us. It cannot establish causation. It cannot account for the policy responses, fiscal space, or structural conditions that shaped each economy’s specific trajectory. It covers only economies with usable data, which excludes some of the smallest and most vulnerable SIDS. It measures the shock and recovery using annual GDP — a blunt instrument that misses within-year variation, employment, and inequality.
What it can do is document, clearly and reproducibly, that the pattern exists — and that the choice of tourism indicator, sample, and measurement approach all matter for how clearly you can see it.

Indicator definitions and sources: Data Dictionary

Analysis conducted using R 4.4.1. Data retrieved November 2026.

text:
Field
Value




Short name
OWID visitor spending


Variable name in analysis
visitor_spend_gdp_pct, baseline vspend_mean_1519 / vspend_mean_1719


Definition
Money received by the destination country from foreign visitors, including spending on accommodation, food, transport, entertainment, shopping, and fares paid to the country’s own airlines, expressed as a percentage of GDP


Units
Percent of GDP


Source
UN Tourism (2025); National statistical organizations and central banks, OECD national accounts, and World Bank staff estimates (2026) — processed by Our World in Data


OWID variable ID
1146095


Date range
1995–2024


Coverage
~200 countries/territories


Raw file
data/raw/spending-by-international-visitors-while-visiting-a-country-as-a-share-of-gdp/


Retrieved
January 2026



This indicator does not correspond to a single WDI indicator code. The numerator (international tourism receipts) comes from UN Tourism statistics collected through annual questionnaires following the International Recommendations for Tourism Statistics (IRTS 2008). The denominator (GDP) comes from World Bank national accounts estimates. Do not attribute this indicator to ST.INT.XPND.GD.ZS or any other unverified WDI code.
Distinction from tourism direct GDP: Visitor spending captures money spent by foreign visitors in a country. This is not equivalent to tourism’s direct contribution to GDP. A dollar spent by a visitor does not translate into a dollar of domestic value added — a portion flows to imported goods and services. Tourism direct GDP (SDG 8.9.1) measures the domestic value-added component only; it is a smaller number and requires Tourism Satellite Account (TSA) methodology to calculate.
Use in analysis: Primary pre-pandemic tourism-dependence indicator. 2015–2019 five-year means used as the primary baseline; 2017–2019 three-year means used as a sensitivity comparison.











Field
Value




Short name
OWID tourism GDP


Variable name
tourism_gdp_pct, baseline tgdp_mean_1719


Definition
Tourism Direct GDP as a share of total GDP. Measures the value created when visitors spend money in the country, expressed as gross value added by all industries serving visitors, plus net taxes on goods and services tourists buy. Tracks SDG 8.9.1.


Units
Percent of GDP


Source
UN Tourism (2025) via Our World in Data


Methodology
Tourism Satellite Account (TSA). Countries without a TSA are absent from this dataset — coverage gaps reflect institutional capacity, not absence of tourism.


Date range
2008–2023


Coverage
~125 countries with TSA data


Raw file
data/raw/tourism-gdp-proportion-of-total-gdp/



Not used as primary indicator in this analysis due to substantially lower coverage (15 of 29 OWID shock sample members have TSA data, vs. 29/29 for the visitor spending indicator). Used as a complementary measure in coverage audits.

This is a volume measure, not an economic dependence indicator. It does not appear in the primary shock regression. It is included in the data for contextual reference.











Field
Value




Short name
WDI tourism receipts


WDI code
ST.INT.RCPT.XP.ZS


Variable name
tourism_receipts_pct_exports, baseline receipts_mean_1519 / receipts_mean_1719


Definition
International tourism receipts as a percentage of total exports of goods and services. Tourism receipts include any payments made to the destination country by tourists for accommodation, food, transport, entertainment, and shopping during their visit.


Units
Percent of total exports


Source
World Development Indicators, World Bank


Date range
~1995–2020 in this retrieval (no observations beyond 2020)


Coverage
~180 countries


Retrieved via
wbstats::wb_data(), November 2026



Note on availability: this series ends at 2020 in the current retrieval. WDI ST.INT.RCPT.XP.ZS contains no observations beyond 2020 in the November 2026 retrieval. The most likely explanation is a change in UN Tourism’s data dissemination approach following the pandemic — much of UN Tourism’s current reporting has moved to interactive data portals — rather than a simple publication lag. The WDI series may no longer be actively updated. Additionally, 2019 data is missing for 14 of 35 WDI shock-sample members — their 2017–2019 baseline is computed from 2017 and 2018 only. Users requiring post-pandemic tracking of tourism receipts should consult the UN Tourism data portal directly.
Distinction from OWID visitor spending: Both series ultimately draw on UN Tourism receipts data, but:

The denominator differs: OWID uses GDP; WDI uses total exports of goods and services.
Their magnitudes and rankings differ accordingly: for export-intensive micro-states, the receipts/exports ratio can be very large; for larger, more diversified economies, it can be small.
The two series are correlated (Pearson r ≈ 0.77, Spearman ρ ≈ 0.86 across the common sample) but not interchangeable.

Use in analysis: Complementary indicator. Used in WDI shock sample (N=35) and common-sample comparison alongside OWID visitor spending.

title: Data Dictionary
text:
Processed Datasets

data/processed/candidates.csv
58-economy candidate universe. Fields: iso3, country, sids_region, sids_status, political_status, source, notes. Authority: UN-OHRLLS list of SIDS, November 2026.


data/processed/country_coverage.csv
Coverage matrix. One row per candidate. Fields include observation counts for each indicator in the 2017–2019 window and binary sample-membership flags (in_primary_shock_sample, in_receipts_shock_sample, in_common_sample, in_recovery_sample).


data/processed/baseline_shock_recovery.csv
One row per economy (51 economies with any WDI data). Contains: 2015–2019 and 2017–2019 baseline means and observation counts for all tourism indicators; 2015–2025 wide-format columns for economic outcomes; sample membership flags.


data/processed/analytical_panel.csv
Long-format panel, 2008–2025, 51 economies × 18 years. All WDI and OWID indicators. Used as the primary input to baseline and recovery calculations.


data/processed/recovery_index.csv
Long-format recovery dataset for primary shock sample (N=29), 2015–2025. Contains gdp_index (real GDP, 2019=100) and gdppc_index (real GDP per capita, 2019=100).


data/raw/worldbank/wdi_tourism_covid.csv
Raw WDI data retrieved via wbstats::wb_data(). Retrieved November 2026. Indicators: ST.INT.RCPT.XP.ZS, NY.GDP.PCAP.CD, NY.GDP.MKTP.KD.ZG, NY.GDP.MKTP.KD, NY.GDP.PCAP.KD, SL.UEM.TOTL.ZS. Years: 2008–2025. 51 economies (7 candidate codes not returned by WB API: AIA, GLP, MTQ, MSR, BES, COK, NIU).


data/raw/worldbank/wdi_retrieval_metadata.txt
Records retrieval date, indicators requested, country codes requested, and codes returned/missing.

title: Data Dictionary
text:
SIDS Classification



Table D1. SIDS universe classification notes.






topic
note




UN SIDS count
UN-OHRLLS lists 39 economies under Small Island Developing States. Of these, 37 are UN General Assembly member states; Cook Islands and Niue are sovereign states in free association with New Zealand and are not UNGA members but ARE included on the SIDS list.


Cook Islands (COK)
Sovereign state in free association with NZ. Member of many UN specialized agencies (WHO, UNICEF, FAO, etc.). Not a UN General Assembly member. Included on UN-OHRLLS SIDS list. Not in WDI database.


Niue (NIU)
Sovereign state in free association with NZ. Member of some UN specialized agencies. Not a UN General Assembly member. Included on UN-OHRLLS SIDS list. Not in WDI database.


Bahrain (BHR)
Was previously on some UN SIDS lists as an AIMS economy. As of the current UN-OHRLLS list (retrieved November 2026), Bahrain is not listed as a SIDS. Not included in the candidate universe.


Associate Members
The 18 associate members listed by UN-OHRLLS are territories and dependencies that are associate members of UN Regional Commissions. They are included in the SIDS group but are not sovereign states. Not all have WDI coverage.


BES
Bonaire, Sint Eustatius and Saba are Dutch special municipalities. Not on the UN-OHRLLS list. Retained in the candidate universe as an other island economy for regional completeness.


Data authority
UN-OHRLLS list of SIDS, retrieved November 2026. URL: https://www.un.org/ohrlls/content/list-sids






Cook Islands and Niue
Both appear on the UN-OHRLLS SIDS list among the 39 listed economies. They are sovereign states but are not UN General Assembly member states — both are in free association with New Zealand. They are members of many UN specialized agencies. Neither has WDI coverage; neither appears in any analytical sample.


Bahrain
Not on the current UN-OHRLLS list (November 2026). Previously appeared on some SIDS lists as an AIMS economy. Not included in the candidate universe.


Non-UN-listed economies
Bonaire, Sint Eustatius and Saba (BES) is retained in the candidate universe as an “Other island economy” for regional completeness. It is not on the UN SIDS list. It has no WDI coverage and does not contribute to any analytical sample.
